entities.name: Dharma
entities.summary: Right order, duty, and righteousness — central to the Gītā.
entities.description: Dharma denotes cosmic and social order, personal duty, and righteousness. The Gītā turns on Arjuna's dharma-crisis on the battlefield of Kurukṣetra.

seo.title: Dharma
seo.description: Duty, righteousness, and cosmic order in the Bhagavad Gītā.

concept.definition: That which upholds — cosmic order, social duty, and righteous conduct.
concept.meaning: In the Gītā, dharma is both the field (dharmakṣetra) and Arjuna's personal duty as a warrior (svadharma), weighed against compassion and confusion.
concept.etymology: From Sanskrit √dhṛ “to hold, sustain” — that which upholds the world and one's role within it.
examples: Arjuna's crisis: fight as kṣatriya dharma vs. killing kin
Kurukṣetra named dharmakṣetra in Gītā 1.1
Yudhiṣṭhira as Dharmarāja — king of dharma

entities.name: Karma
entities.summary: Action and its consequences; taught as Karma-yoga in the Gītā.
entities.description: Karma is action. In the Bhagavad Gītā, Kṛṣṇa teaches acting without attachment to fruits (karma-yoga).

seo.title: Karma
seo.description: Action and karma-yoga in the Bhagavad Gītā.

concept.definition: Action; also the law linking deeds to their results.
concept.meaning: The Gītā reframes karma as disciplined, detached action offered without clinging to outcomes — the path of karma-yoga.
concept.etymology: From Sanskrit √kṛ “to do, make” — deed, work, ritual act.
examples: Gītā 2.47 — right to action, not to fruits
Karma-yoga as sacrifice of action to the Divine
Niṣkāma karma — desireless action

entities.name: Bhakti
entities.summary: Devotional love of the Divine; a central path in the Gītā.
entities.description: Bhakti is loving devotion. The Gītā presents devotion to Kṛṣṇa as a path of liberation alongside knowledge and action.

seo.title: Bhakti
seo.description: Devotional love as a path in the Bhagavad Gītā.

concept.definition: Loving devotion and surrender to the Divine.
concept.meaning: Bhakti-yoga is the path of the heart — worship, remembrance, and offering — presented as accessible and supreme in the later Gītā chapters.
examples: Chapter 12 — the devotee dear to Kṛṣṇa
Offering leaf, flower, fruit, or water in love (9.26)
Constant remembrance and surrender

entities.name: Jñāna
entities.summary: Liberating knowledge of the Self and the Absolute.
entities.description: Jñāna is discriminative wisdom. In the Gītā it is the path of knowing the eternal Self (ātman) and its relation to Brahman, distinct from mere information.

seo.title: Jñāna
seo.description: Knowledge-yoga and wisdom in the Bhagavad Gītā.

concept.definition: True knowledge — insight into Self, reality, and liberation.
concept.meaning: Jñāna-yoga is the path of understanding: discriminating the eternal from the transient, and seeing the one Self in all beings.
examples: Kṛṣṇa teaching the eternal Self beyond the body
Jñāna-yajña — sacrifice of knowledge (ch. 4)
Field and knower of the field (ch. 13)

entities.name: Yoga
entities.summary: Discipline of union — action, knowledge, and devotion in the Gītā.
entities.description: Yoga in the Bhagavad Gītā means disciplined practice uniting the self with the Divine through karma, jñāna, and bhakti.

seo.title: Yoga
seo.description: Disciplined union in the Bhagavad Gītā.

concept.definition: Disciplined union of the self with the Divine.
concept.meaning: In the Gītā, yoga is not only posture but skill in action, evenness of mind (samatva), and paths of karma, jñāna, and bhakti.
examples: Samatvaṃ yoga ucyate — evenness is called yoga
Karma-yoga, jñāna-yoga, bhakti-yoga as paths
Dhyāna-yoga of chapter 6 — meditation

entities.name: Ātman
entities.summary: The eternal Self — beyond body, mind, and death.
entities.description: Ātman is the innermost Self. The Gītā teaches that the Self is unborn, eternal, and untouched by the death of the body — the ground of Arjuna's courage.

seo.title: Ātman
seo.description: The eternal Self in the Bhagavad Gītā.

concept.definition: The true Self — eternal consciousness beyond body and mind.
concept.meaning: Kṛṣṇa teaches that weapons cannot cut the Self, fire cannot burn it; grief over death of bodies is born of ignorance of ātman.
concept.etymology: Sanskrit ātman — breath, self, essence; the reflexive “oneself”.
examples: Gītā 2 — the Self does not die with the body
“I am the Self seated in the hearts of all” (10.20)
Knower of the field (kṣetrajña) as Self

entities.name: Brahman
entities.summary: The Absolute — ultimate reality taught in the Gītā and Upaniṣads.
entities.description: Brahman is the impersonal Absolute. The Gītā speaks of knowing Brahman, becoming Brahman-like (brahma-bhūta), and the relation of ātman to the highest.

seo.title: Brahman
seo.description: The Absolute in the Bhagavad Gītā.

concept.definition: Ultimate reality — the Absolute underlying all that exists.
concept.meaning: Distinct from Brahmā the creator-god, Brahman is the ground of being. The Gītā links liberation with resting in Brahman and seeing Kṛṣṇa as its personal face.
concept.etymology: From Sanskrit √bṛh “to expand, grow great” — the vast, the Absolute.
examples: Akṣara Brahman — the Imperishable (ch. 8)
Brahma-nirvāṇa — peace in Brahman
Identity and distinction of ātman and Brahman in teaching

entities.name: Māyā
entities.summary: Divine creative power and the veil that binds the soul.
entities.description: Māyā is the Lord's wondrous power and the illusion that conceals true nature. The Gītā speaks of divine māyā that is hard to cross without taking refuge.

seo.title: Māyā
seo.description: Divine power and illusion in the Bhagavad Gītā.

concept.definition: The Divine's creative power and the appearance that veils reality.
concept.meaning: Not mere 'falsehood' — māyā is Kṛṣṇa's own energy that projects and binds; crossing it requires devotion and knowledge.
concept.etymology: Sanskrit māyā — art, wonder, illusion, measuring-out.
examples: Divine māyā hard to transcend (Gītā 7)
Guṇas of prakṛti as binding appearance
Refuge in the Divine as the way beyond māyā

entities.name: Prakṛti
entities.summary: Primordial nature — the field of the three guṇas.
entities.description: Prakṛti is material nature. In the Gītā's Sāṅkhya teaching, all action belongs to prakṛti and its guṇas; the Self is the witness.

seo.title: Prakṛti
seo.description: Material nature and the guṇas in the Bhagavad Gītā.

concept.definition: Primordial nature — matter and energy of manifestation.
concept.meaning: Paired with puruṣa, prakṛti is the changing field of the three guṇas (sattva, rajas, tamas). Actions arise in prakṛti; the wise do not claim doership.
examples: Three guṇas binding the embodied soul (ch. 14)
Lower and higher prakṛti of the Lord (ch. 7)
Field (kṣetra) as prakṛti in chapter 13

entities.name: Puruṣa
entities.summary: Conscious spirit — the knower paired with prakṛti.
entities.description: Puruṣa is the conscious principle. The Gītā's Sāṅkhya and Vedānta strands treat puruṣa as the witness Self, and the supreme Puruṣa as the Lord.

seo.title: Puruṣa
seo.description: Spirit and the supreme Person in the Bhagavad Gītā.

concept.definition: Conscious spirit — the knower and witness of nature.
concept.meaning: In Sāṅkhya, puruṣa is plural conscious selves amid prakṛti. In the Gītā, the supreme Puruṣa (Puruṣottama) is Kṛṣṇa beyond the perishable and imperishable.
concept.etymology: Sanskrit puruṣa — person, man, cosmic Person (Ṛgvedic sense).
examples: Knower of the field as puruṣa (ch. 13)
Puruṣottama — the supreme Person (ch. 15)
Two puruṣas: perishable and imperishable
